quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten checks on the three shedding mechanisms and the conventions of point paper.

questions.q: How many heald frames does a tappet (cam) shedding mechanism normally control?
questions.explain: A tappet controls about 6–8 heald frames and repeats of up to 8 picks. 14–20 (up to 28) frames is the range of a dobby.

questions.q: A dobby typically controls how many heald frames?
questions.explain: Dobbies handle 14–20 frames and some up to 28, enough for cords, piqué, honeycomb and small figures. Controlling every end individually is the jacquard's job.

questions.q: What does a jacquard control?
options: Every warp end individually, through hooks
questions.explain: A jacquard lifts each end by its own hook, so there is no limit from heald frames; that is what makes figured fabrics, damask and brocade possible.

questions.q: A tappet loom is the usual choice for weaving piqué and honeycomb.
questions.explain: Piqué, honeycomb, huckaback and cords need more frames and longer repeats than a tappet's 6–8 frames and 8 picks allow; they are dobby weaves.

questions.q: Damask and brocade with large motifs are woven on which mechanism?
questions.explain: Large motifs need individual control of hundreds of ends, which only a jacquard gives. A dobby is limited to repeats that fit in its frames.

questions.q: On point paper each vertical column of squares represents:
questions.explain: Columns are ends and rows are picks. Heald frames and dents belong to the draft and denting plans, not to the weave drawing itself.

questions.q: A filled (black) square on point paper means:
options: The pick lies over the end
The end is lifted over that pick, so warp shows on the face
The end and pick are tied
questions.explain: Filled = end up (warp on the face); empty = pick over end (weft on the face). Reversing this convention turns the whole design over.

questions.q: On point paper the first pick is drawn at the top and the first end on the right.
questions.explain: The convention is first pick at the bottom and first end on the left, so the drawing is read upward and rightward like a graph.

questions.q: The repeat of a weave is:
options: The smallest block of ends and picks that tiles the whole cloth
The full width of the point paper
The number of picks a tappet can weave
questions.explain: A weave is drawn as one repeat, the smallest block that can be copied side by side and up and down to cover the cloth. Point paper is often drawn larger only to show the tiling.

questions.q: What decides how many heald frames a design needs?
options: The number of picks in the repeat
The number of different end movements in the design
questions.explain: Ends that move identically can share a frame, so the number of distinct end movements sets the frame count. A design needing more frames than the loom has must go to a dobby or jacquard.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: Limits of each mechanism, how repeats tile, and how a weave's lifting order shows on point paper.

questions.q: A tappet can weave repeats of up to how many picks?
questions.explain: Tappet repeats run up to 8 picks, with 6–8 frames. 28 is the maximum frame count of a large dobby, not a tappet limit.

questions.q: A design needs more heald frames than the loom has. What must happen?
options: Weave it anyway with fewer frames
Move it to a dobby or jacquard loom
questions.explain: Frames cannot be shared by ends that move differently, so the design must go to a mechanism with enough capacity. Changing sett or count does not change the number of movements.

questions.q: One repeat of plain weave is 2 ends × 2 picks.
questions.explain: Every end alternates over and under and the second pick is the opposite of the first, so the pattern repeats after two ends and two picks even though it is often drawn on 8 × 8.

questions.q: In a 3/1 twill, how does the lifting pattern change from one pick to the next?
options: It shifts one end to the right
It shifts three ends to the right
questions.explain: Each end is up for 3 picks and down for 1, and every pick moves the pattern one end along, producing the diagonal. Reversing completely is plain weave.

questions.q: An empty square on point paper tells you that on that pick:
options: The weft lies over the end, so weft shows on the face
The warp is on the face
questions.explain: Empty means the pick lies over the end: weft on the face at that crossing. The weft is always inserted; the square only records which thread is on top.

questions.q: A weave with a 4 × 4 repeat is drawn on 8 ends × 8 picks. How many full repeats does the drawing show?
questions.explain: 8 ÷ 4 = 2 repeats across and 2 repeats up, 2 × 2 = 4 repeats in all. Counting only one direction gives the common wrong answer of 2.

questions.q: In plain weave, how does pick 2 relate to pick 1?
options: It is shifted one end to the right
It is the exact opposite: every end that was up is down
questions.explain: Plain weave alternates: odd ends up on pick 1, even ends up on pick 2. A one-end shift is the twill rule, not plain weave.

questions.q: Which weave shows the largest proportion of warp on its face?
questions.explain: In 3/1 each end is up on 3 of 4 picks, so 75 % of the face is warp. Plain weave is 50 % and 1/3 only 25 %; 1/3 is the back of 3/1.

questions.q: An 8 × 8 drawing of a 3/1 twill contains two repeats in each direction.
questions.explain: The 3/1 twill repeats on 4 ends and 4 picks, so 8 × 8 holds two repeats across and two up, which is why the lecture labels it 'fabric effect (2× repeat)'.

questions.q: A honeycomb design has 10 distinct end movements and a 10-pick repeat. What is the smallest mechanism that can weave it?
questions.explain: 10 movements exceed a tappet's 6–8 frames and the repeat exceeds 8 picks, but a dobby with 14–20 frames handles it easily. A jacquard would be unnecessary cost.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Counting squares, repeats and heald frames on point paper for plain weave and 3/1 twill.

questions.q: Plain weave is drawn on 8 ends × 8 picks. How many squares are filled?
questions.explain: Plain weave lifts half the ends on every pick: 8 × 8 = 64 squares, half of them filled = 32.

questions.q: A 3/1 twill is drawn on 8 ends × 8 picks. How many squares are filled?
questions.explain: Each end is up on 3 of every 4 picks, so three-quarters of the 64 squares are filled: 48.

questions.q: In one 4 × 4 repeat of a 3/1 twill, how many ends are lifted on each pick?
questions.explain: Each pick lifts 3 of the 4 ends (one end is down per pick), which is why 3/1 is called warp-faced.

questions.q: A 2 × 2 plain-weave repeat is tiled over a block of 16 ends × 12 picks. How many repeats does the block contain?
questions.explain: 16 ÷ 2 = 8 repeats across and 12 ÷ 2 = 6 repeats up; 8 × 6 = 48 repeats.

questions.q: What percentage of the face of a 3/1 twill is warp?
questions.explain: Up 3 picks out of 4 means 3 ÷ 4 = 75 % warp on the face; the remaining 25 % is weft.

questions.q: A 3/1 twill has four ends in its repeat and every end moves differently. How many heald frames does it need?
questions.explain: The repeat has 4 ends, each with a different lifting order, so 4 frames are needed, well within a tappet's capacity.

questions.q: A dobby has 20 heald frames. A design has 24 ends per repeat but only 6 distinct end movements. How many frames are left spare?
questions.explain: Frames are set by distinct movements, not repeat width: 6 frames used, 20 − 6 = 14 spare.

questions.q: In a 3/1 twill on 4 ends, pick 1 lifts ends 1, 2 and 3. Which ends are lifted on pick 3?
questions.explain: Each pick shifts one end to the right: pick 2 lifts 2, 3, 4; pick 3 lifts 3, 4 and wraps round to 1. Ends 4, 1, 2 would be pick 4.

questions.q: How many squares are filled in a single 4 × 4 repeat of a 3/1 twill?
questions.explain: 4 picks × 3 ends up per pick = 12 filled squares out of 16.

questions.q: A 1/3 twill (the back of 3/1) is drawn on 8 ends × 8 picks. How many squares are filled?
questions.explain: Each end is up on only 1 pick in 4, so one-quarter of 64 squares are filled: 16. Turning a 3/1 drawing over swaps filled and empty.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Choosing the right loom for an order and avoiding point-paper mix-ups on the shop floor.

questions.q: A mill with only tappet looms receives an order for huckaback towels. What should the production manager do?
options: Weave it on the tappet looms
Book it on dobby looms, in-house or at a partner mill
Change the order to plain weave
questions.explain: Huckaback is a dobby weave; a tappet's 6–8 frames and 8-pick limit cannot handle it. A jacquard would work but is needless expense for a small repeat.

questions.q: A weaver has a 12-frame dobby. A new design has 16 distinct end movements. Which option is realistic?
options: Weave it with 12 frames by leaving 4 ends out
Redesign to 12 or fewer movements, or move it to a larger dobby or jacquard
Weave it on a tappet instead
Increase the picks per inch so the frames are shared
questions.explain: Every distinct movement needs its own frame. Dropping ends changes the design; sett has no effect on frame count; a tappet has even fewer frames.

questions.q: A buyer wants a brocade tablecloth with a large floral motif. Which shedding mechanism must be quoted?
questions.explain: Large figured motifs need individual end control, which is a jacquard. Dobbies only manage small figures that fit within their frames.

questions.q: A dobby loom can weave plain weave and simple twills as well as its more complex designs.
questions.explain: Any weave whose repeat fits the frames can be woven on a dobby, including plain weave on 2 frames. Mills usually reserve dobbies for designs the tappets cannot handle because dobby time costs more.

questions.q: A designer draws a 3/1 twill with pick 1 at the top of the paper, but the weaver reads it bottom-first as usual. What happens to the cloth?
options: Nothing — the pick order does not matter
The twill diagonal runs the opposite way (Z becomes S)
The warp face becomes weft face
questions.explain: Reading the picks in reverse order reverses the direction of the shift, so the diagonal leans the other way. The face is unchanged because filled squares still mean end up.

questions.q: Which is the cheapest shedding mechanism able to weave a plain 3/1 drill?
questions.explain: A 3/1 twill needs 4 frames and a 4-pick repeat, well inside a tappet's range, and tappet looms are the simplest and cheapest to run.

questions.q: A design has a 12-pick repeat and 14 distinct end movements. A mill has 8-frame tappet looms and 28-frame dobby looms. Where does it go?
options: Only a jacquard can weave it
Neither — the repeat is too long
questions.explain: 14 movements and 12 picks exceed the tappet (8 frames, 8 picks) but fit a 28-frame dobby comfortably. A jacquard is not needed.

questions.q: The lecture draws plain weave on 8 × 8 squares even though its repeat is 2 × 2. Why?
options: Because 2 × 2 is too small to weave
To show how the repeat tiles and what the fabric effect looks like
Because point paper only comes in 8 × 8
questions.explain: The larger drawing is a 'fabric effect' showing several repeats side by side. The weave itself, and the frames it needs, come from the 2 × 2 repeat.

questions.q: A student fills squares where the weft passes over the end instead of where the end is lifted. What will the woven cloth show?
options: The design turned over: face and back swapped
Nothing — the loom will not run
questions.explain: Inverting the convention inverts every lift, so the cloth is woven with its back on top. A 3/1 twill would come out as 1/3, for instance.

questions.q: A design needs 9 heald frames and has a 10-pick repeat. Why can it not go on a tappet loom?
options: Both the frame count and the pick repeat exceed what a tappet handles
It can — tappets handle up to 28 frames
questions.explain: A tappet manages 6–8 frames and repeats up to 8 picks; this design fails on both counts and needs a dobby. 28 frames is the top of the dobby range.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions on repeats, frame counts and the logic of point paper, including the slips students most often make.

questions.q: The lecture's 3/1 twill drawing is labelled '8 ends × 8 picks, fabric effect (2× repeat)'. How many repeats does it contain altogether?
questions.explain: '2×' refers to each direction: two repeats across and two up make four in total. The true repeat is 4 × 4.

questions.q: A weave repeats on 6 ends and every end moves differently. How many heald frames does it need?
questions.explain: With no two ends moving alike, each end needs its own frame: 6 frames, still within a tappet's range if the pick repeat is 8 or less.

questions.q: Why does the back of a 3/1 twill look like a 1/3 twill?
options: Because wherever warp is on the face, weft is on the back, so the proportions are reversed
Because the loom weaves two cloths
questions.explain: Every filled square on the face is an empty square seen from the back. Three-quarters warp on the face means three-quarters weft on the back: a 1/3 twill.

questions.q: Which statement about point paper is correct?
options: Rows are ends and columns are picks
The first pick is at the bottom and a filled square means the end is lifted
A filled square means the weft is on the face
The first end is on the right
questions.explain: Columns are ends, rows are picks, pick 1 at the bottom, end 1 on the left, filled = end up. The other three options each reverse one part of the convention.

questions.q: A jacquard does not use heald frames at all; each end is lifted by its own hook.
questions.explain: That individual control is the whole point of the jacquard: there is no frame limit, so figured fabrics with very large repeats can be woven.

questions.q: A 3/1 twill shifts one end to the right on each successive pick. On point paper with pick 1 at the bottom, in which direction does the diagonal run?
options: From lower left to upper right
From upper left to lower right
questions.explain: Each higher row is displaced one column to the right, so the filled squares climb from bottom-left to top-right, a Z-direction twill.

questions.q: A 3/1 twill drawn on 8 × 8 has 48 filled squares. How many empty squares does the same drawing have?
questions.explain: 8 × 8 = 64 squares; 64 − 48 = 16 empty squares, one per end per repeat where the weft is on the face.

questions.q: A 10-end weave has 10 distinct end movements and a 10-pick repeat. A mill offers an 8-frame tappet, a 16-frame dobby and a jacquard. Which is the most economical loom that can weave it?
questions.explain: Ten frames and ten picks are beyond the tappet but fit a 16-frame dobby. The jacquard could do it but at higher cost for a small repeat.

questions.q: A student counts the rows of a point-paper drawing and reports the number of ends. What has gone wrong?
options: Rows are picks; the ends are the columns
Ends cannot be counted on point paper
The drawing must be turned over first
questions.explain: Columns are warp ends and rows are picks. Swapping them would also swap the warp and weft counts and the frame calculation, so the mix-up matters.

questions.q: In a 2 × 2 plain-weave repeat, end 1 is up on pick 1 and down on pick 2. What is end 2 doing on pick 2?
questions.explain: Pick 2 is the opposite of pick 1: end 1 down, end 2 up. Every end alternates and every pick alternates, so the four squares form a chequerboard.
